articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit
articles.context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On October 21, 2026, we observed participants in underground forums seeking PHP2Shell exploits, while others shared scripts presented as exploiting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Discussion included doubts about prerequisites and whether circulating code worked. This post examines that gap between interest, claimed capability, and verified exploitation.

Our assessment covers selected forum posts and messages collected as of October 21. The findings show what was being discussed and shared, rather than confirmed compromises.

Forum participants requested exploit material, shared code, and questioned each other’s claims. For the security industry, this is a reminder to share threat findings promptly across security teams, researchers, and vendors so defenders can assess emerging threats and coordinate their response.

Looking for an exploit they could trust

Exploit.in is a long-running, primarily Russian-language underground forum where participants discuss hacking techniques and trade tools and services. Monitoring these discussions can reveal interest in emerging vulnerabilities and questions about available exploits.

“Does anyone have it?” was the question, translated from Russian, in a discussion on Exploit.in naming both PHP2Shell CVEs. The request sought exploit material, while subsequent comments questioned the prerequisites and legitimacy of circulating PoCs. One participant wrote “Didn’t test but seems legit.” A further comment described code execution “with preconditions,” while referring to a different “real exploit.” These are participant opinions about the circulating material, not our technical conclusions.

The exchange in Figure 1 captures both demand for an exploit and doubts about whether the available code worked. It leaves open whether the requester ever obtained a working exploit.

Figure 1. PHP2Shell exploit requests and discussion observed on October 21, 2026.

What circulated on October 21

On October 21, we recorded an English-language technical writeup at 02.23 UTC whose author claimed a lab reproduction. Hebrew- and Persian-language messages recorded at 05.16 and 05.35 UTC shared security alerts about the vulnerabilities and upcoming patches. The language of a post does not tell us where its author is based. At 06.22 UTC, we recorded a separate Exploit.in post presenting scripts as exploits for both CVEs, shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2. Forum post presenting purported PHP2Shell exploits, observed on October 21, 2026.

We redacted exploit instructions and memory offsets to avoid sharing details that could help reproduce an attack. The screenshot preserves the forum context.

A separate screenshot shared in a monitored channel appeared to show command execution on a local test system. We have not independently verified the result, and its exact posting date was unavailable.

By October 21, our searches returned 68 forum posts for PHP2Shell / CVE-2026-109618 and 62 for CVE-2026-109618. Chat searches returned 81 messages for PHP2Shell and 57 for CVE-2026-109619. These figures measure discussion volume in the collected material. The searches overlap, so the counts are not a combined total.

The forum exchanges show participants openly requesting exploit material, sharing code, and questioning each other’s claims. Separately, security alerts circulated in several languages across monitored messaging channels. Together, these observations illustrate how quickly information about a vulnerability can spread. For defenders, they reinforce the value of timely information sharing across organizations and language barriers, with clear distinctions between observed activity, unverified claims, and validated findings.

Public analysis offers context on PoC reliability

Public technical discussion published on October 23 on the SANS Internet Storm Center website examined why some circulating PoCs depended on specific server settings and knowledge of the target environment. The discussion concerned the PoCs reviewed there, rather than every possible way to exploit PHP2Shell.

The public analysis suggests that the PHP version, server setup, and information available to an attacker can affect whether a PoC works. These dependencies may help explain the questions raised in the forum thread.

Connecting intelligence with observed attempts

In our separate traffic analysis, we observed exploitation attempts, scanning, and invalid-PoC attempts. The invalid-PoC attempts add context to the forum discussion about whether circulating code worked. We detail these findings in our published PHP2Shell exploitation and IPS research. We have found no evidence connecting those requests to the forum participants or scripts discussed here.

We continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update our protections as exploitation techniques evolve. Our cloud-delivered IPS signatures blocked exploitation attempts on inspected customer traffic without requiring a separate protection package. PHP services outside our inspection coverage require separate remediation and protection. Updating affected PHP installations remains essential.

The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks.

articles.title: Cato CTRL Research on Suspected Iranian MuddyWater Activity Using Israel Tax Authority Lures and SimpleHelp
articles.context: The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

We investigated a campaign targeting Israeli organizations through phishing emails impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. The activity has been observed since September 2026. Government-themed domains and a verification page lead recipients to ZIP archives containing executables disguised as tax-related documents. The campaign abuses SimpleHelp, a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, to enable attacker-directed remote access.

The lure exploits a routine business task and can reach finance, accounting, and administrative staff across sectors. We suspect a connection to MuddyWater based on its documented use of SimpleHelp and targeting of Israel.

Key Findings

The campaign uses Israel Tax Authority impersonation and government-themed domains to distribute ZIP archives to Israeli organizations.

The payload is presented as a tax-related document but is a SimpleHelp executable.

Cato telemetry recorded threat prevention alert against campaign web infrastructure. The event demonstrates prevention of that request, without establishing a completed remote-access session.

Attack Flow

Figure 1 summarizes the delivery chain. Remote access depends on successful execution and activation of the SimpleHelp component.

Figure 1. Tax authority impersonation leads to a SimpleHelp executable. The dashed final step represents potential remote access following successful execution.

Technical Details and Analysis

This activity was previously described in public reporting by CyberIL. Our investigation examined the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and use of SimpleHelp.

From a tax themed email to a verification page

The attack begins with a phishing email impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients attempting to access the supposed personal area are directed to a lookalike site and prompted to complete a CAPTCHA-style verification step before downloading a ZIP archive.

The infrastructure uses names such as document-govil[.]com to resemble the official Israeli government namespace, gov.il. The string govil is part of a separately registered domain and does not indicate government affiliation.

The verification page in Figure 2 displays a checkbox, a Continue button, and the password 123123. This presentation reinforces the appearance of a protected document-delivery process.

Figure 2. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure.

A ZIP archive delivers the executable

Following the verification step, the download is presented as a tax-related archive. Figure 3 shows Israel_Tax_Authority.zip in the browser download history. The investigation also identifies an archive named document.zip.

Figure 3. Download of Israel_Tax_Authority.zip.

The agency-themed naming continues inside the archive. The executable shown in Figure 4 is named רשות המסים בישראל.exe, meaning “Israel Tax Authority.” A recipient expecting a tax document is instead presented with a program to run. The payload inventory also includes document.exe.

Figure 4. Executable named רשות המסים בישראל.exe presented under the tax authority pretext.

SimpleHelp provides the remote access capability

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software. In this campaign, it is used as the remote-access component behind the document lure. The research identifies 129.121.120[.]121 as associated command-and-control infrastructure.

Successful deployment can allow an operator to connect to the endpoint and continue the intrusion using the software’s built-in capabilities. The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact. It describes capabilities rather than observed post-compromise actions.

Potential attacker use

Broader endpoint compromise and operational disruption

More targeted follow-on activity

Faster and repeatable intrusion activity

Unattended Remote Access Service

These capabilities are described in SimpleHelp’s feature documentation, Toolbox Guide, and Remote Access Guide.

The activity involved social engineering and abuse of legitimate RMM functionality. Our findings and SimpleHelp’s assessment are summarized in the disclosure section below.

Mapping the infrastructure with FOFA

We searched FOFA for the two observed HTTP ETag values. The search returned eight service records associated with 129.121.120[.]121, including records for document-govil[.]com and document-govil[.]online, as shown in Figure 5. Both domains displayed “Coming Soon” pages served by nginx.

Figure 5. FOFA results linking the two domains to 129.121.120[.]121. The eight results are service records on one IP.

Public reporting on SimpleHelp abuse

Group-IB previously documented MuddyWater’s use of SimpleHelp, providing context for our attribution assessment. Sophos, CISA, and Huntress have also reported separate ransomware incidents involving SimpleHelp exploitation or abuse.

Attribution Assessment

We suspect MuddyWater involvement based on the combination of Israeli organizational targeting, locally tailored authority impersonation, and delivery of legitimate remote-access software through phishing. HarfangLab documented an October 2023 MuddyWater phishing email linking to a SimpleHelp installer. Proofpoint documented Hebrew payroll lures in March 2024 that led Israeli recipients through PDF links to ZIP archives containing Atera installers.

Earlier campaigns also used institution-themed Egnyte subdomains and Hebrew filenames related to scholarships and tourism. These examples show a recurring approach of adapting recognizable Israeli identities and routine business tasks to persuade recipients to install remote-access software. The current campaign follows a similar pattern through Israel Tax Authority impersonation and tax-themed filenames.

The February 2022 joint government advisory identifies MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

Disclosure Timeline

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Based on the evidence reviewed and validation with SimpleHelp, we did not identify exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability or compromise of SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure in connection with this campaign. The activity investigated involved social engineering intended to induce users to deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure, consistent with the broader abuse of legitimate RMM tools by threat actors.

SimpleHelp confirmed that both samples identify themselves as SimpleHelp Remote Access Client version 5.4.5. Based on the information we provided, SimpleHelp assessed the activity as apparent malicious use of an older release and stated that it had not seen evidence indicating exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability. SimpleHelp offered to investigate associated infrastructure and assess available action, requesting server addresses or hostnames, observation timestamps, and supporting evidence through a private file request. We subsequently shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp.

Date

We reported the campaign and associated SimpleHelp abuse to SimpleHelp.

20-OCT-2026

SimpleHelp identified both samples as Remote Access Client version 5.4.5, reported no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the information provided, and requested infrastructure details to investigate.

21-OCT-2026

We shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp for investigation.

Cato Protection

Cato automatically blocks the campaign domains and IOCs listed below, protecting Cato customers against these identified threats without requiring manual indicator updates.

In addition, Cato MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring, investigation, and response for suspicious activity involving remote-access tools and attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Figure 6 shows a Cato IPS event with the action recorded as Block for a request to document-govil[.]com/Form/Forms/, with destination IP 129.121.120[.]121.

Figure 6. Cato telemetry showing an IPS Block event against campaign infrastructure.

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Research: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts in the Wild, and How Cato IPS Blocked Them
articles.context: The first scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared on 21 October, the day the fixes were released, and about two thirds of all attack sources in our sample first appeared that day
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On 21 October 2026, PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, a pair of critical runtime vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell. One day later, we described how our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent turned the patch into reviewed IPS protection in minutes. This report follows what happened next, including how quickly attackers moved, what their attempts looked like, and how Cato’s cloud-delivered IPS protection blocked them on inspected customer traffic.

Key findings

Attempts started on patch day. We observed no external PHP2Shell-pattern requests from 17 to 20 October. The first scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared on 21 October, the day the fixes were released, and about two thirds of all attack sources in our sample first appeared that day.

Cato IPS blocked both exploitation attempts and scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. In the sample analyzed, about 41% of blocked attempts were exploitation attempts aimed at remote code execution (RCE), and 59% were scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. About 96% of all hits related to CVE-2026-109618.

Exploitation attempts fell into two main types. Command-execution attempts were the most common, followed by deserialization attempts.

A handful of sources drove most attempts. In our sample, a small number of source IPs generated most of the blocked attempts, repeating proof-of-concept (PoC) style requests.

Attempts appear opportunistic, not sector-focused. Healthcare made up about one third of the organizations that received blocked attempts, but the same sources reached unrelated sectors and countries.

Introduction

PHP2Shell is a pair of flaws in the PHP core runtime rather than in a single application or plugin. CVE-2026-109618 concerns out-of-memory handling that can interrupt request initialization and leave invalid data for cleanup to process. CVE-2026-109619 concerns request-owned state that is retained after its memory is freed and later accessed by the same worker. Both can lead to unauthenticated code execution, and the highest demonstrated risk is in Apache mod_php, where exploitation can occur before any application code runs.

In our first threat brief, Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed, we described how our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent built a PoC and generated IPS signatures in minutes, with researcher review before release. At that point, our initial telemetry showed scanning activity only.

This follow-up answers the questions security teams ask next. Once the patch was public, how fast did attackers move, what did they try, and did protection keep up? We look at timing, attempt types, sources, the industries that received attempts, and the tooling involved.

Methodology

We queried a sample of anonymized, aggregated Cato cloud security telemetry from 17 to 26 October 2026 for inbound requests matching the PHP2Shell pattern and our PHP2Shell IPS protections. We group blocked attempts into two categories, exploitation attempts and scanning or invalid-PoC attempts. The second category covers simple scanning as well as exploit attempts that used false or invalid proofs of concept. Results are shown as approximate percentages, and industries are grouped so that no individual organization can be identified.

Limitations

Sample-based. The figures reflect a sample of Cato-inspected traffic, not global internet activity, and show the shape of activity rather than exact volumes.

Attempts, not outcomes. This research describes attempted attacks, not compromises.

Geolocation is not attribution. Source country reflects where an IP is hosted, often a cloud or VPS provider, not who operates it.

Technical insights

1. Timeline from silence to patch-day onset

Figure 1 shows the clearest finding. From 17 to 20 October, we observed no external requests matching the PHP2Shell pattern. On 21 October, the day PHP published its fixes, the first external scanning or invalid-PoC attempt appeared in the morning, and that day accounts for about 72% of the PHP2Shell-pattern requests in our sample. This is consistent with Amazon Threat Intelligence, which reported proof-of-concept exploits circulating on 21 October. Amazon also reported a single exploitation attempt against its own honeypots on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. We saw no such pre-disclosure activity in Cato customer traffic.

Figure 1. Daily share of external PHP2Shell-pattern requests across the observation window.

Daily volume is spiky because one noisy scanner can dominate a day. A better measure of how activity spread is when each attack source first appeared. In Figure 2, 100% represents all attack sources observed during the study window. About two thirds of them first appeared on 21 October, and new sources appeared on most days after.

Figure 2. Attack sources by first-seen date, as a share of all sources observed in the window.

Hour by hour, 21 October unfolded in two phases (Figure 3). A few early scanning or invalid-PoC attempts in the morning were followed in the afternoon by a single source sending a burst that made up about 80% of the day’s requests. Later in the day, activity fanned out, with about 40% of the day’s sources active within a single hour, which is typical of a PoC circulating and many operators running it at once.

Figure 3. Share of requests and of active sources per hour on 21 October.

2. From scanning and invalid PoCs to code execution attempts

In the sample analyzed, about 96% of blocked attempts related to CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory flaw, and about 4% to CVE-2026-109619. About 59% were scanning or invalid-PoC attempts, and 41% were exploitation attempts aimed at remote code execution (Figure 4). Some attempts relied on PoCs that were not valid against the vulnerable code path, so we grouped them with scanning activity. Exploitation attempts fell into two main types, command execution and deserialization, with command execution the more common.

Figure 4. Blocked PHP2Shell attempts by CVE and by intent, based on a sample of Cato telemetry.

3. Source geography

Based on a sample of the sources we observed, the United States leads by share of source IPs (about 36%), followed by the Netherlands and Germany (about 14% each). By share of blocked attempts, US-hosted sources account for about 54%, the Netherlands about 18% and Moldova about 16% (Figure 5). Activity was concentrated, with a small number of sources generating most of the blocked attempts in the sample.

Figure 5. Source IP geolocation by share of sources and share of blocked attempts, based on a sample of sources.

4. Who received the attempts

Blocked attempts reached organizations across a broad range of industries (Figure 6). Healthcare and social care is the largest group at about one third, followed by technology and security services. The remainder is spread across professional services, automotive, education and non-profit, and other sectors, in several countries.

Figure 6. Industry mix of the organizations that received blocked attempts.

Does the healthcare share mean healthcare was singled out? The evidence suggests not. The same sources sent attempts to healthcare organizations and to unrelated sectors in different countries. For example, a single source reached healthcare, technology and software organizations on the same day. The sample is small, and the share may also reflect the composition of our customer base. One plausible explanation is shared technology. PHP-based portals, forms and line-of-business applications are common across many industries, including healthcare.

Additional recommendation

Cato customers do not need to deploy anything for PHP2Shell protection. The IPS signatures are delivered and enforced from our cloud. We also recommend updating every PHP instance to the fixed version released by the PHP project.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell showed how short the window between patch and attack has become. We saw no PHP2Shell-pattern traffic for four days, then scanning or invalid-PoC attempts on the day the fixes were released, followed by exploitation attempts. The attempts were automated, repetitive and opportunistic, reaching organizations across many industries and countries. With a runtime-level bug, the deciding factor is whether an organization exposes PHP, not which industry it is in.

Dedicated PHP2Shell signatures, built by our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent and reviewed by our researchers, blocked exploitation attempts on inspected traffic. Because enforcement happens in the Cato cloud, customers did not need to install anything, and this virtual patching reduces exposure while application owners upgrade.

This research covers a sample of attempts on inspected traffic, not outcomes, during the first days after disclosure.

We will continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update protections as attacker techniques evolve.

articles.title: See the Real AI Experience with Cato DEM
articles.context: From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate Detecting poor performance is only the first step
articles.full_text:
AI is becoming part of everyday work. Employees rely on services such as ChatGPT and Claude to research, create, and solve problems, while developers increasingly use AI-powered tools like Cursor and coding agents in their development workflows.

As employees increasingly rely on AI to work more productively, the AI experience is becoming a critical part of the digital experience IT teams are expected to support. Slow responses, failed interactions, or inconsistent performance can disrupt workflows and undermine the productivity gains AI is meant to deliver.

The challenge is that IT may have limited visibility into the AI interaction itself. Teams may not know there is a problem until employees start complaining.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) addresses this visibility gap with AI Experience Monitoring, providing IT teams with live visibility into AI latency and failures, along with the context they need to investigate performance problems.

AI Is Becoming Critical to Everyday Work. Can IT See When It Fails?

As AI becomes embedded in daily workflows, its performance increasingly affects employee productivity. An employee waiting on ChatGPT or Claude, or a developer relying on an AI coding tool, expects that interaction to work quickly and reliably.

That creates a new digital experience for IT teams to support.

But knowing that an AI application is reachable does not necessarily tell IT whether the actual AI interaction is performing well. Teams may only learn about slow responses or failed interactions when a user opens a ticket saying, “Claude is slow today.”

Then the investigation begins. Is the issue associated with a particular AI service or model provider? Is it concentrated at a specific location? Does it affect users accessing the service in a particular way?

The challenge for IT is no longer simply whether employees can reach an AI service. It is knowing whether the AI experience is working well, before employees must tell them it isn’t.

Traditional Application Monitoring Can Obscure the Real AI Experience

Monitoring an AI application is not the same as monitoring an employee’s interaction with the AI model.

GenAI applications such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor generate many different types of network traffic. The agentic portion of that traffic, including conversational interactions with AI models and traffic from coding agents, can be mixed with software downloads and updates, authentication requests, licensing and configuration calls, telemetry, and other background activity.

Measuring all this traffic together can create a noisy representation of the actual AI experience. For example, a large application download may affect usage figures even though it has nothing to do with an employee’s conversation with an AI model. Performance measurements can similarly mix model-provider latency with unrelated application activity.

As a result, IT can see application traffic without getting clean answers to two fundamental questions: How quickly is the AI responding, and how often are AI interactions failing?

To understand the real AI experience, IT needs to separate this AI traffic from the surrounding application noise.

Isolate the AI Traffic That Matters with Cato DEM

Cato DEM addresses this challenge with AI Agent Experience Monitoring.

Instead of treating all traffic generated by a GenAI application as a single experience, Cato isolates the AI portion of that traffic, the interactions with AI model providers, including conversational traffic and traffic from coding agents such as Claude Code. By separating these AI interactions from downloads, updates, authentication, telemetry, and other background traffic, Cato gives IT a clearer view of the experience that matters to users.

The capability focuses on two fundamental indicators: latency, showing how quickly the AI service is responding, and errors, showing how often AI interactions are failing.

IT can examine performance by application and model-provider domain to identify where degraded experiences are occurring. At launch, coverage includes ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, with additional AI services to be added over time.

And because AI Agent Experience Monitoring is built directly into Cato DEM, AI performance becomes part of the same digital experience monitoring environment IT teams already use.

Instead of waiting for someone to report that “AI is slow,” IT gains live visibility into the AI traffic itself.

From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate

Detecting poor performance is only the first step. IT also needs context to narrow the investigation.

Cato provides a dedicated AI Agent Experience Monitoring drill-down, where teams can analyze latency and errors by model provider, domain, and site. They can also see how employees are accessing the AI service.

Cato DEM also shows how users access AI services, whether through a browser, terminal, script, or coding tool. For example, IT can distinguish between someone accessing Claude through a browser and a developer using a coding tool such as Claude Code.

Consider that complaint: “Claude is really slow today.”

Without AI-specific experience visibility, IT starts with a broad application-level investigation where model interactions are mixed with other Claude traffic. With Cato DEM, teams can focus on latency and failures in the actual AI traffic and then use provider, site, and client context to narrow the investigation.

This turns a vague user complaint into a much more focused performance investigation.

Cato DEM measures the network experience of that traffic; it does not monitor what an AI agent does.

Catch Poor AI Experiences Before They Become User Complaints

AI is becoming another digital tool employees rely on to get work done. Cato DEM gives IT teams the visibility to support that experience proactively.

Teams can identify slow AI interactions without background application traffic obscuring the picture. They can spot failed interactions through error monitoring. And when something goes wrong, the provider, site, and access context give IT operations and network teams a more focused starting point for troubleshooting.

Most importantly, this visibility lives within DEM alongside the performance data that the performance data teams already monitor. IT can extend the same operational approach used to support other employees’ digital experiences to AI services, making them part of everyday work.

As AI becomes increasingly important to employee productivity, waiting for users to report poor performance is no longer enough. Cato AI Agent Experience Monitoring helps IT see the real AI experience, so teams can find slow or failing AI before users must tell them something is wrong.

For detailed configuration guidance, refer to the Cato Knowledge.

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform
articles.context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform appeared first on Cato Networks
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys were compromised after being generated with insufficient randomness. Attackers could use these keys to forge certificates and impersonate legitimate websites or services to clients that still trust them. An attacker able to intercept a connection could potentially read or modify sensitive traffic.

We have deployed a certificate-trust update through our centrally managed PoP architecture, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Delivering the update through the Cato Cloud removed the need for customers to patch security appliances at individual locations.

What happened?

Intermediate CAs sign certificates used to authenticate websites and services. Compromising their private keys can enable attackers to issue fraudulent certificates for domains they do not control. Organizations can therefore face exposure even when their legitimate certificates come from another provider.

Google and Mozilla received reports on October 17, 2026, and distributed emergency certificate blocks that day.

Mozilla also released updates associated with CVE-2026-113470. These include the certificate block list directly in Firefox and Thunderbird, protecting installations even when automatic block-list updates are disabled or unavailable.

Google found that no website certificates issued through the six affected TLS intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs before its emergency block took effect. CT logs are public records of certificates. Browsers that enforce CT, including Chrome, require valid proof that a certificate has been submitted to these logs before accepting it. Those browsers would therefore have rejected fraudulent certificates from the affected intermediates even before receiving the emergency blocks.

However, this protection does not extend to all software. Some applications, older browsers, or configurations without CT enforcement may have accepted unlogged fraudulent certificates if they still trusted the affected intermediates. The absence of certificates from those intermediates in CT logs before Google’s block therefore does not prove that no attacks occurred.

eMudhra says its root private keys and other intermediate CAs are unaffected. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Business risks

The exposure extends beyond employee browsers. Applications, API integrations, containers, and embedded devices may use independent trust stores or lack effective certificate-revocation checks.

Potential business consequences include:

Credential theft and data exposure: Intercepted connections could expose passwords, session tokens, and confidential information.

Transaction manipulation: Attackers impersonating trusted services could alter business communications or API responses.

Service disruption: Emergency trust removal can also reject legitimate certificates. Google announced a broader root-removal rollout expected on October 27, requiring affected website operators to replace their certificates.

Operational costs: Identifying and updating separate trust stores across applications and infrastructure creates work and opportunities for missed remediation.

These are potential impacts, not evidence of observed exploitation.

Our response: centralized control, global enforcement

The Cato AI-native SASE Platform converges networking and security in a cloud-native service delivered through globally distributed points of presence (PoPs). Our Single Pass Cloud Engine provides integrated security enforcement, while centralized management allows us to deliver updates across our cloud infrastructure. This reduces the coordination and maintenance work customers would otherwise undertake across distributed security appliances.

Centralized operations also support controlled deployment. Our established PoP change-management practices include phased rollouts, validation, monitoring, and rollback capabilities to manage operational risk as the platform evolves.

What this means for our customers

We have centrally deployed a certificate-trust update across our globally distributed PoPs, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Customers do not need to make configuration changes to receive this update.

Analysis of our data lake showed that the certificate chains affected by this update appeared in only a very small proportion of the network flows examined. Based on this limited usage, we expect minimal connectivity impact for customers.

For details about the update and potential connectivity impact, see the security update.

For locations or connections that access the internet outside our platform, organizations should apply the relevant vendor updates or extend our platform’s coverage so those connections are subject to our certificate-validation controls.

articles.title: Why so many AI security programs start with the OWASP Top 10
articles.context: What OWASP is The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners
articles.full_text:
When an auditor or an RFP asks how your organization handles AI risk, the OWASP Top 10 lists are often a core part of the checklist behind the question. Cato AI Security is built to address the risks on two lists.

What OWASP is

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners. It publishes free security guidance, and volunteers lead its projects and local chapters worldwide.

Its GenAI Security Project publishes several lists. Two of the most widely used are the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2026) and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026). Each list ranks the 10 most critical risks that an AI security program should cover. Many security teams treat the lists as an industry standard and plan their AI security work around them.

The LLM list covers applications with a model embedded inside them, where risks include prompt injection and sensitive data leaking in a response. The agentic list covers what changes once agents plan tasks and call tools on their own.

The OWASP lists give each AI Security team the same set of risks to work from:

App developers use them as a guide to the risks their applications should avoid.

Security vendors build their products around them.

Auditors use them to assess the risk in an AI platform.

Buyers use them to evaluate AI security platforms.

Mitigating those risks is a responsibility shared by the security vendor and the teams that build and run your AI apps and agents. A security platform can stop some risks on its own. Others also need work in the app, the data pipeline or the agent platform.

How Cato AI Security maps to OWASP

Cato AI Security covers the risks on both lists in three ways:

Direct protection: Cato stops the risk in line, before the AI application or agent acts.

Shared protection: Cato reduces the risk and works with your app developers on the rest.

Platform evidence: Cato logs every AI interaction in an audit-ready format, so your team can investigate and show auditors what happened.

Cato AI security runs AI Security for Users, Applications, and Agents with unified visibility, context, and control, so the same inspection and policy applies to every risk below. The OWASP risks fall into three groups.

Supply chain risks

AI apps and agents rely on models, MCP servers and skills that someone else built. If one of them is compromised, every agent that uses it inherits the problem. OWASP lists this as Supply Chain (LLM04) and Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04).

A security team can’t set a policy for tools it can’t see. Cato protects against supply chain risk by discovering MCP servers and skills connected to agents and coding tools, including ones IT never approved, and applying policy to each one.

Prompt injection and sensitive data exposure

Attackers can hide instructions in content a model or agent reads and make it act against your policy. Employees can also paste API keys or personal data into an AI app. OWASP lists these as Prompt Injection (LLM01), Agent Goal Hijack (ASI01) and Sensitive Information Disclosure (LLM02).

Cato AI Security protects against prompt injection and data exposure through runtime guardrails on AI agents and the custom applications your teams build. It inspects each prompt and response in line, along with the results tools send back to an agent. Cato blocks prompt injection and jailbreak attempts before the model or agent acts.

The same inspection finds sensitive data in prompts and responses and in files attached to AI apps.

Tool misuse and excessive agent access

An agent with access to tools can change records and run commands. If it has more access than it needs, one bad instruction can cause serious damage. OWASP lists these as Excessive Agency (LLM03), Tool Misuse and Exploitation (ASI02) and Unbounded Consumption (LLM06).

Cato AI Security lets your security team name the tools, MCP servers and skills an agent may use, and block or monitor each one. Your security team can also set limits on how much apps and agents spend on model usage.

Where your team’s work starts

Some risks sit partly outside the traffic path. For these types of risks, Cato AI Security works alongside your team or provides platform evidence:

Data and model poisoning (LLM05): Cato AI Security detects manipulated context in live interactions, while your data pipeline owners protect training and fine-tuning data.

Rogue agents (ASI10): Cato AI Security keeps an inventory of agent activity and applies policy to each agent in line, while your agent platform owns the kill switch.

Cato’s AI interaction logs sit beside network, cloud access security broker (CASB) and endpoint data on one platform, so an analyst doesn’t have to pull logs from separate tools to investigate.

Get the full mapping from your Cato representative

Talk to your Cato representative to receive the complete map of how Cato covers the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We’ll go through the OWASP lists with you and map them against the apps and agents you run today, one use case at a time. You’ll see our coverage for each risk and how we work with your team to mitigate each one.

articles.title: Cato AI Endpoint secures browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents on every endpoint
articles.context: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware
articles.full_text:
AI used to live in a browser tab. Today it also runs inside the apps employees use every day, like Copilot in Word, in dedicated apps like ChatGPT and in coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Coding agents work differently from chat apps. A chat app answers a question and waits. A coding agent is given tools and takes actions on its own, with the developer’s access.

So every endpoint is becoming an agentic endpoint. Your security team now needs to know what the AI on those endpoints does and whose data it touches.

Cato AI Endpoint is a lightweight client that secures AI in the browser, AI in desktop apps and the coding agents developers run locally.

Separate point products leave blind spots on the endpoint

Take two employees on an ordinary afternoon. Sam, a developer, asks a coding agent to tidy up a build.

The agent opens the project files and reads the passwords inside. Then the agent pulls in a tool or a skill your security team never approved.

Maya in finance pastes a customer list into the ChatGPT app because she wants a summary before her next meeting. Neither Sam nor Maya means any harm.

Most of today’s security tools miss both. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware.

The web filter watches the browser, and network tools see what leaves the endpoint.

Sam’s agent works inside the endpoint, so much of what it does doesn’t cross the network at all. Maya’s prompt does leave, but some AI desktop apps lock their connection to their own certificate (certificate pinning), so network tools can’t look inside their traffic. The customer list goes out, and your security team doesn’t see it.

Each of those tools still does the job it’s made for, but network security can’t see enough of the endpoint to control agentic AI.

Skills and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are add-ons that give agents extra abilities, and skills and MCP servers that sit installed but unused still widen the attack surface. An employee installs a skill once and forgets it, but the agent decides when to use it. If that skill can make web requests, the agent can use it to send data anywhere without asking.

Adding another point product for each kind of AI doesn’t close the gap either. Each product leaves its own blind spots and splits policy enforcement across more tools.

Secure browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents together

Cato AI Endpoint protects local agents, desktop apps, embedded AI assistants and web AI traffic with a lightweight client, so teams deploy and manage fewer tools. Protection starts with knowing which AI is already on your endpoints.

Discover Shadow AI and Agents. Shadow AI is AI that employees use without approval. Cato AI Endpoint can find the AI applications, local agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints, so your security team knows what is in use and what to govern first.

Protect Prompts and Responses Inline. When Sam’s agent calls the unapproved tool, Cato AI Endpoint can block the tool before it runs. The rest of the agent’s work carries on.

Cato AI Endpoint doesn’t act while Maya types or pastes. When Maya sends the prompt, Cato AI Endpoint can inspect and block the prompt on the endpoint before the customer list reaches the AI model. Maya sees a pop-up saying company policy blocked the prompt, and her session carries on.

The same user interaction rule applies to AI in the browser and desktop apps, with no extra configuration. When a prompt is sent, the rule can monitor it, block it or anonymize it by swapping names and other sensitive data for placeholders. Coding agents get monitor and block controls, and your team manages browser, desktop and coding agent protection from one dashboard.

Add AI security without replacing your existing stack

You’ve invested in EDR, in SSE (the cloud security service that includes your web filter) and in a VPN, and you can’t afford to disrupt them. You also need AI protection now.

Cato runs alongside the existing security stack. Only AI application traffic goes to Cato, and all other traffic stays on your existing tools, so you can see the AI in use within weeks.

The Cato AI Endpoint client goes out through device management like any other app. Finding the agents on an endpoint requires no network change. If another SSE client already runs on the endpoint, your team sets up both clients to run side by side.

Catch risky agents and prevent unsafe actions

Blocking Sam’s tool stops one unsafe action. Your security team also needs to know which other agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints are risky.

The Cato AI Endpoint client gives each skill a risk finding with a block, monitor or allow recommendation. Verified remote MCP servers get a badge. Cato can also flag risky agents, MCP servers and skills before they act, so teams can fix the riskiest first.

A week later, when someone asks which AI touched customer data, your team opens one dashboard and finds Sam’s blocked tool next to Maya’s blocked prompt. Each shows the user, endpoint and data behind it. Endpoint and network AI events sit in the same platform and data lake, so they share context.

Sam gets a tidy build without the unapproved tool, and Maya’s customer list stays inside the company.

For more details, read the solution brief or check the Cato AI Endpoint page and book a demo.

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief on Attacks Against Refrigeration Controllers
articles.context: Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

CERT-FR’s October 13 update reports compromises of refrigeration controllers, naming Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC alongside Copeland/Dixell XWEB systems. The entry methods remain unconfirmed. CERT-FR warns that attacks are probably continuing and recommends removing public exposure, checking configurations, and securing remote access. Compromised operational technology (OT) can disrupt cooling, compromise stored products, and threaten cold-chain continuity.

Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. This work supported deployment of IPS signatures within 24 hours of the initial incident reports as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings across refrigeration vendors to assess the need for additional signatures.

Operational and business impact

Operational disruption. Unauthorized changes to setpoints, defrost schedules, or alarms can disrupt cooling across multiple units, spoil products, and delay detection.

Business and supply-chain impact. Inventory losses, interrupted sales, equipment damage, and emergency maintenance can cause financial and reputational harm. At scale, disruption could affect food availability and national resilience.

Security exposures to assess

Internet-exposed management interfaces. Publicly reachable controllers face greater risk of unauthorized access where authentication and access restrictions are inadequate.

Remote access without least privilege. Shared accounts, weak authentication, and excessive permissions increase the risk of unauthorized changes. Access across sites and weak segmentation can widen the impact.

Vulnerable or unsupported systems. Published research into Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWEB Pro controllers documented multiple vulnerabilities. Their exploitation in the reported attacks has not been confirmed.

Overlooked cellular connections. Supplied SIMs and vendor-managed 4G/5G routers may bypass network controls and escape inventories, monitoring, and risk assessments. Private APNs also need verified isolation between subscriber devices.

How Agentic AI Can Accelerate OT Attacks

Agentic AI could accelerate reconnaissance, analysis of disclosed vulnerabilities, and repeated exploitation attempts against reachable controllers. This may reduce the time and expertise needed to turn an exposed interface into operational disruption. At the time of writing, we have not identified public evidence of AI involvement in the refrigeration incidents.

Protection and recommendations

General recommendations

The following are general recommendations for reducing risk across connected refrigeration environments.

Reduce internet exposure. Remove unnecessary public access. Authenticate and authorize remote users before granting equipment access through a secure VPN or protected network, following CERT-FR guidance.

Secure maintenance access. Change default passwords. Use unique credentials, named accounts, MFA where supported, and least privilege, separating monitoring from configuration access where possible.

Maintain supported systems. Track firmware and support status, apply vendor updates, and replace unsupported equipment. Follow Danfoss security guidance and guidance for other deployed platforms.

Segment operational equipment. Allow only required traffic between refrigeration equipment, corporate IT, maintenance networks, and sites.

Monitor operating conditions. Alert on unexpected changes to temperatures, defrost schedules, alarms, and accounts. Consider independent temperature monitoring and verify safe operation after incidents.

Assess cellular access. Inventory SIMs and vendor-managed cellular links. Include them in risk assessments, verify access controls and logging, and validate private APN isolation and routing.

Cato protection

Our SASE platform supports authenticated remote access, least-privilege access policies, and network segmentation. SASE allows these controls and traffic inspection to be managed centrally across sites and remote maintenance connections routed through the platform. In a previous blog post, we discussed OT security recommendations and showed how the platform supports secure remote access, segmentation, and monitoring of device communications.

In another previous blog post, we discussed how Cato Autonomous Policies for FWaaS analyzes policy rules and their context to help identify misconfigurations and overly permissive access.

Our Researcher Agent helped us create a proof of concept for Danfoss controller vulnerabilities, supporting our mitigation work. This agent-assisted workflow helps accelerate vulnerability analysis and protection development while retaining researcher review.

IPS virtual patching provides network-based protection against applicable vulnerability exploitation. Coverage depends on the vulnerability, enabled controls, and traffic reaching the relevant inspection point.

In another blog post, we discussed how our Agentic Threat Prevention correlates suspicious host activity and applies inline controls to help interrupt attack progression, including lateral movement. This is relevant where a compromised system could provide a route toward operational equipment or other connected assets.

We have added IPS signatures for applicable, publicly disclosed Danfoss vulnerabilities as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings involving Danfoss and other refrigeration vendors. As new information becomes available, we will assess the need for additional IPS signatures and updates to our virtual patching coverage.

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed
articles.context: How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially...
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On 21 October 2026, PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution. Cato’s self-evolving CVE mitigation agent helped turn the investigation into concrete research output by creating a proof of concept and generating an IPS signature in minutes. The agent connects vulnerability analysis, controlled lab testing and protection generation. Validation feedback and researcher corrections inform improvements to its skills and workflows, while security researchers review proposed protections before release. Cato has put PHP2Shell IPS protections in place, connecting fast agentic research with cloud enforcement to help customers reduce exposure on inspected traffic while they update affected applications.

Why Cato AI native SASE enables protection at machine speed

Speed matters because attackers can study the same patches defenders use. Our AI-native SASE approach connects our self-evolving agentic CVE mitigation researcher with centralized cloud inspection and enforcement. The researcher helps turn vulnerability analysis into candidate signatures, with validation and security researcher review before release. We can then deliver protections through our cloud without customers installing a separate signature package on each PHP server. This shortens the path from disclosure to protection while application owners complete remediation.

What happened

The flaws affect PHP core rather than a single application or plugin. PHP identifies installations serving web requests as at risk, including PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The highest demonstrated risk is in Apache mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs. A login page therefore does not reliably shield the vulnerable processing.

CVE-2026-109618 concerns out-of-memory handling that can interrupt initialization and leave invalid request data for cleanup to process. CVE-2026-109619 concerns request-owned state retained after its memory is freed and later accessed by the same worker. These failures can lead to code execution. Sensitive process memory may also be exposed. Exploitability depends on the runtime integration, configuration and reachable behavior.

The UK NCSC urged immediate action to identify PHP installations and apply updates. NHS England’s alert highlights code execution and sensitive memory exposure, while Canada’s Cyber Centre also calls for assessment of products that bundle PHP. These official advisories reinforce the urgency of remediation.

The business risk

Public research also shows unauthenticated code execution on tested WordPress, Drupal and Joomla deployments, and separate disclosure of PHP worker memory. These examples illustrate runtime exposure. Exploitability varies by deployment.

For a business, code execution could expose application data, allow content changes or disrupt customer-facing services within the PHP process’s permissions. Memory disclosure could reveal passwords, tokens and API keys even without code execution. Usable credentials could extend the risk to connected services. Prioritize systems by exposure, sensitive data and the business processes they support.

How our self evolving researcher agent built signatures in minutes

Once the PHP fixes became available, we analyzed the changes and found behavior that appeared materially different from the publicly circulated alleged exploit. This prompted additional research before finalizing the signatures. The discrepancy did not establish whether that material described another issue or an incomplete attack path.

Our self-evolving CVE mitigation agent created a proof of concept (PoC) and generated an IPS signature in minutes. The new signatures address the alleged scenario and the patch-analysis findings, with coverage bounded by the attack paths tested.

Our agentic researcher combines vulnerability intelligence, patch analysis and controlled testing to develop candidate IPS protections. Its self-evolving workflow uses validation feedback, execution traces and researcher corrections to refine the skills and workflows used in subsequent investigations. Our security researchers review proposed protections before release, bringing expert judgment to the path from generated signature to customer protection. Figure 1 shows this workflow from patch analysis and PoC creation to signature validation, researcher review and cloud enforcement.

Figure 1. Self-evolving CVE mitigation from patch analysis to PoC, signature and enforcement.

PHP2Shell from PoC to signature in minutes

In Figure 2, the upper pane shows the local PHP2Shell test completion message, while the lower pane shows runtime monitoring and test events. This capture comes from the investigation in which our agent created a PoC and generated a signature in minutes. Detailed outcomes are redacted.

Figure 2. PHP2Shell PoC test and runtime monitoring. Results redacted.

Cato protection

Our infrastructure assessment found that Cato’s production systems are not exposed to PHP2Shell. This finding concerns the infrastructure we operate.

For customer environments, we have added PHP2Shell IPS signatures covering the alleged scenario and additional behavior identified through patch analysis. These protections help block matching exploit requests on traffic inspected by our cloud when the applicable signatures are enabled in blocking mode. Customers should also assess and update affected PHP applications and third-party products in their environments.

The connection to Agentic Threat Prevention (ATP) is the speed of turning evidence into enforcement. Our CVE mitigation researcher uses vulnerability evidence to create signatures after disclosure. ATP evaluates related host activity as an attack develops and activates prevention policies to restrict its next steps.

In our separate controlled demonstration against an agentic attacker, ATP used shared context and inline controls to prevent progression to full domain compromise. The PHP2Shell response described here delivered CVE-specific IPS signatures. Together, these examples show how AI-native SASE can accelerate both the creation of protections and adaptive enforcement during an intrusion.

Our initial response telemetry showed scanning, with no exploitation attempts identified against customers.

The attacker path and where we block it

Figure 3 illustrates a hypothetical PHP2Shell attack and how our IPS protection would apply. It places an attacker on the left, our cloud IPS in the center and a vulnerable PHP service on the right. The crafted request represents an attempt to exploit the PHP runtime. The red stop mark shows where a matching request would be dropped when payload inspection and the applicable blocking protection are active. Some exploit paths involve multiple requests.

Figure 3. Illustrative PHP2Shell attack path and IPS prevention.

The diagram illustrates our protection model rather than documenting an observed customer attack. Traffic must pass through our cloud with its payload visible to inspection and the applicable signature enabled in blocking mode.

Close coverage gaps

Identify PHP services outside our inspection coverage. Extend our inspection coverage and blocking where supported. Protect remaining gaps with an appropriate application-layer control, such as an inbound WAF configured for PHP2Shell. Continue updating affected PHP runtimes.

The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: Cato AI native SASE delivers PHP2Shell protection at machine speed appeared first on Cato Networks.

articles.title: Make Your SIEM Smarter with Cato
articles.context: Network outages and cyber threats demand real-time responses, making timely insights critical
articles.full_text:
Effective security operations require more than isolated alerts. Analysts need context from across the environment to understand what happened, assess its significance, and decide what to do next. That is why accessing insights and telemetry from across your networking and security stack is critical to teams using a SIEM tool. That wider context from endpoints, identity, cloud, applications, network infrastructure, and threat intelligence, brought into a common operational workflow, adds essential intelligence. With more complete information available where analysts already work, they can investigate faster and make better-informed decisions.

Cato XOps brings network and security context from across the Cato SASE Platform into a shared operational view to accelerate incident detection, investigation, and response. Organizations can use that context in the operating model that works best for them, by enriching their existing SIEM workflows with the Custom HTTP Push Connector, or by bringing network and security operations closer together with Cato XOps.

Add Cato Context to SIEM Workflows

Most security operations teams have invested heavily in their SIEM: detection rules, investigation processes, automation, and the expertise to use them well. However, legacy approaches too often rely on scheduled collection or polling for updated data. Network outages and cyber threats demand real-time responses, making timely insights critical. Adding Cato telemetry strengthens the existing operating model, without creating another place to work. Cato context can be analyzed alongside endpoint, identity, cloud, and other telemetry they already available in the SIEM. When suspicious activity appears, analysts can investigate with Cato data in the same investigation workflow, reducing time spent moving between tools and providing more context to access scope and potential impact.

Send the data that each destination needs

Different destinations require different Cato data.

A SIEM used for security investigation may need a different set of Cato data than a platform used for network analytics or long-term analysis. Organizations can align the data sent to each destination with how it will be used. Full control over the source, destination, filters and context. There’s even a data dictionary to demystify endless fields of information, translating them to help find what matters.

Control Ingestion and Retention

Filtering data before it is sent helps keep relevant telemetry available to analysts while reducing unnecessary SIEM ingestion. It also supports destinations such as long-term storage and custom analytics.

Use Case: See More Context. Detect and Investigate Faster.

Consider an analyst investigating suspicious user activity in an existing SIEM. The SIEM may already correlate signals from identity and endpoint tools, but analysts often need additional network and security context to understand what happened and assess the potential impact.

When the SIEM flags suspicious activity, analysts can use Cato telemetry alongside existing identity and endpoint data without switching workflows.

That approach supports several parts of security operations.

Investigate with more context. Add relevant Cato network and security telemetry to the data already used for detection and correlation in the SIEM, reducing the need for separate tools. Less noise, more insights.

Leverage network data to stop attacks quicker. Up to 70% of breaches use lateral movement, so by including network insights alongside security event data, IT teams understand the complete attack path, and can respond and remediate faster.

Extend existing workflows. Feed Cato data into existing threat hunting, analytics, and automation processes instead of creating parallel processes around another data source.

Configure filters before sending to SIEM.

Use Case: Consolidate your responses with Cato XOps

For organizations without a SIEM, or who are looking to bring their network and security teams together for even faster, more efficient operations, Cato XOps supercharges incident response.

That context extends beyond traditional north-south security visibility. The majority of data breaches involve lateral movement across the network. Because Cato also sees east-west traffic across the WAN, analysts can gain signals associated with activity moving between enterprise resources, adding network context that security-focused data sources alone may not provide. The majority of Cato XOps also brings unique benefits around more efficient data storage in SIEM solutions. Cato XOps correlates thousands of raw events into consolidated, context rich stories, simplifying what is passed to the SIEM. Where SIEM costs are calculated based on data ingestion volumes, that can help deliver significant savings. One Cato customer turned 37 million daily event logs into just 94 stories.

Use Case: Analytics that’s build around your needs

Every organization has different workflows and environments, and data requirements. The Cato Custom HTTP Push Connector lets organizations define the destination, select Events and Flows, apply filters, and start streaming data.

Alongside the native integrations from Cato , the Connector extends data portability to even more sources. That can also include long term retention, such as in AWS S3, or custom analysis.

Native integrations, bespoke connections or leveraging XOps for the insights and response layer – Cato gives security and network teams flexible ways to provide the right context where it delivers the most value. Native integrations are available for over 100 vendors including CrowdStrike, Microsoft and Open AI, while the Custom HTTP Push Connector streams selected Events and Flows to compatible destinations. Combined with Cato XOps, these capabilities can enrich investigations, manage SIEM ingestion, and extend network and security intelligence across existing operations.

articles.title: Stop Guessing. Find the Root Cause with Cato DEM.
articles.context: RCA brings together the broad range of experience signals available across Cato DEM, along with additional context from the Cato Management Application (CMA), to identify the...
articles.full_text:
When a user says, “the application is slow,” IT has to answer a much harder question: where did the problem actually begin? The issue could be on the endpoint, local network, ISP, the network path, enterprise infrastructure, or application provider itself.

That investigation often takes time because teams have to reproduce intermittent problems, collect evidence from separate tools, and hand cases between endpoint, network, and application owners. By the time troubleshooting starts, the evidence behind a transient issue may already be gone.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) Root Cause Analysis (RCA) changes that workflow. RCA brings together the broad range of experience signals available across Cato DEM, along with additional context from the Cato Management Application (CMA), to identify the likely fault domain and give IT a clearer place to investigate next.

The result is a more evidence-driven troubleshooting process: less time assembling the story after the fact, clearer ownership when issues cross teams, and a faster path from a vague user complaint to a focused investigation.

When “It’s Slow” Doesn’t Tell IT Where to Start

To an employee, very different problems can feel exactly the same. A weak Wi-Fi connection, last-mile congestion, a network path issue, or SaaS provider degradation may all result in the same complaint: “It’s slow.”

For IT, the challenge is not simply confirming that the experience was poor. It is determining where the experience likely broke down and which team should investigate first. A single complaint can span multiple technology domains, while many monitoring tools expose only fragments of that path.

This is especially difficult with intermittent issues. A user may report a frozen video call or a slow application after the condition has already cleared. If the team must recreate the problem before it can collect useful evidence, troubleshooting starts with a disadvantage.

Cato DEM RCA Turns Evidence Into a Starting Point

Cato DEM brings Root Cause Analysis directly into the digital-experience workflow. Instead of leaving administrators to reconstruct the troubleshooting picture manually, RCA correlates endpoint, network, application, and historical path evidence in a single investigation.

The goal is practical: turn available telemetry into a defensible starting point. RCA helps administrators identify the likely fault domain and determine where to act next. That may mean resolving the issue within the current team or routing it once, with supporting evidence, to the team best positioned to investigate.

For help desk, network, and digital workplace teams, that can reduce repeated testing and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth between owners. The investigation begins with context that has already been captured, rather than with a fresh search for clues.

RCA is therefore not another silo of telemetry. It is the layer that makes DEM evidence more actionable.

New Evidence Makes RCA More Actionable

RCA already draws on a broad set of DEM and CMA signals. Network Adapter Metrics and Client Traceroute add two more sources of evidence to the same RCA workflow.

Network Adapter Metrics adds endpoint and local-connectivity context, including adapter type, BSSID, channel, noise, and signal strength. This helps IT assess whether local conditions such as Wi-Fi are contributing to a poor experience.

Client Traceroute adds historical hop-by-hop path evidence from the client. It can reveal latency, loss, and path behavior that might otherwise disappear before the investigation begins, making it particularly useful for intermittent and remote-user issues.

The important point is that administrators do not have to treat these as standalone diagnostics and manually correlate the results. Both enrich the same RCA workflow with additional native context.

From “Zoom Is Freezing” to a Focused Investigation

Consider a remote employee who reports, “My Zoom calls keep freezing.” Without correlated evidence, IT may need to test the device, Wi-Fi, ISP, corporate network, and application provider one at a time.

With Cato DEM, RCA can bring together Network Adapter Metrics, Client Traceroute, in-tunnel traceroute, UCaaS or Real User Monitoring experience data, and network and Cato context in one investigation. Instead of starting with every possible domain, the team gets a likely fault domain and a focused place to begin.

RCA can also look beyond the individual user who triggered the investigation. Correlating experience data from other users can help determine whether the issue is isolated or shared and reveal the broader blast radius of the problem. For example, the evidence may point the investigation toward local Wi-Fi conditions. In another case, path evidence may show that the issue should be routed elsewhere. Either way, IT can start from evidence rather than guesswork.

Less Detective Work Across the Network You Already Have

By preserving and correlating evidence, RCA can accelerate triage, clarify ownership, reduce unnecessary handoffs, and help restore user productivity sooner. The operational shift is simple: teams spend less time finding and assembling evidence and more time acting on it.

That value does not require customers to replace their existing network. Digital-experience issues often cross technology and network boundaries, and Cato DEM is designed to provide visibility and RCA across Cato SASE and supported third-party network environments.

Organizations can begin with a focused troubleshooting use case and expand the shared evidence layer over time. Cato DEM helps IT move from “something is slow” to “here is where to investigate” – with the evidence already in hand.

Please visit the Cato DEM product webpage. For detailed information, refer to the Cato Knowledge Base.

articles.title: Beyond Deployment: Evaluating the Operational Impact of an SD-WAN Refresh
articles.context: Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently
articles.full_text:
Many SD-WAN refreshes start with an expiring contract or edge equipment reaching end of life. But replacing the edge should not be the measure of success.

For network and infrastructure leaders, the real test is what improves after the refresh. Will the refresh put IT on another appliance cycle, or move the WAN to a cloud service? Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently? Can the WAN respond when network conditions change? Can the team support new locations and changing requirements without creating more operational work?

The answers depend on how the new WAN is built and run.

Decide first whether the WAN runs on hardware or in the cloud

An appliance-based refresh replaces old boxes with new ones. IT still patches that hardware at every site, and the replacement cycle starts again when the new boxes reach end of life.

A cloud-delivered SD-WAN moves routing and policy into a cloud service. The device at each site connects the site to that service.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, the Cato Socket at each site connects automatically to the nearest Cato Point of Presence (PoP). The Cato SASE Cloud Platform handles routing and policy enforcement, and Cato maintains the software that runs it. New capabilities can reach every site through the cloud service without a hardware upgrade.

Where the WAN runs shapes the rest of the refresh. The next three sections cover application priority, path control, and day-two work, and each one depends on where the WAN runs.

When you compare SD-WAN options, start by asking whether the refresh puts IT on another appliance cycle or moves the WAN to a cloud service.

Application priority should follow traffic past the branch

SD-WAN can prioritize important applications and steer traffic across available links. But in many architectures, that prioritization stops at the branch.

Once traffic leaves the branch, the application still has to cross the middle mile (the long-haul path between sites and clouds) to reach another site, a datacenter, or the cloud. If bandwidth gets tight along that path, the priority IT set at the branch should still count.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT defines application-aware quality of service (QoS) centrally. Cato applies that priority at the Cato Socket and within the Cato SASE Cloud Platform, so the priority follows traffic into the middle mile. Business-critical traffic can stay at the front of the queue when capacity runs short.

Next, ask whether application priority ends at the branch or follows the application across the WAN.

The WAN should improve the path applications take

Priority can’t fix a bad route, though. A critical application can have the highest QoS priority and still perform poorly if its traffic runs into latency and packet loss on a long route to the destination. Path quality is the second middle-mile problem, after priority.

Cato sends traffic over the Cato Global Private Backbone, which gives Cato more control over the path between sites, clouds, and applications than a WAN that depends primarily on best-effort public Internet routing. Cato monitors network conditions and can route around degraded links across backbone paths between Cato PoPs. Critical applications can keep performing when a backbone path slows down.

For SaaS and public-cloud applications, Smart Egress adds another routing choice. IT can define application-level policy so selected traffic exits from a Cato PoP close to the application instance serving the organization. The traffic stays on the backbone for more of the trip, so employees can see faster response times from those applications.

Then ask whether the WAN can improve the route to the application, or whether the middle mile stays largely outside its control.

A refresh should reduce day-two operations work

Much of the work in an SD-WAN lifecycle happens after deployment.

New branches, policy changes, software updates, troubleshooting, and changing bandwidth requirements all create ongoing work. If that work still happens box by box and site by site, a refresh may replace the hardware without changing the operating model.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT manages routing and application policy centrally through the Cato Management Application, while Cato Sockets support zero-touch deployment at new locations.

Because the WAN runs as a cloud service, IT can spend less time on the patch and replacement cycles that appliance-based designs require.

Finally, ask how much day-two work each option still leaves with your team.

Measure the refresh by what improves after deployment

Newer edge infrastructure is the minimum an SD-WAN refresh should deliver.

Performance and operations are only part of the refresh decision. You also need to decide whether the WAN should secure remote users and cloud access, or leave that job to a separate security stack.

The right choice gives IT a WAN that keeps improving long after the new edge goes in.
